content: A sneeze is a semi-autonomous, convulsive expulsion of air from the lungs. It occurs when particles bypass the nasal hairs and reach the nasal mucosa, triggering the release of histamines. These histamines stimulate nerve cells in the nose, which send a signal to the brain to initiate the sneeze reflex. The brain responds by creating a large opening in the nasal cavity to expel the irritants. This can result in symptoms such as tinnitus, reduced high-frequency hearing, or, in severe cases, a ruptured eardrum. Sneezes are also a significant mode of disease transmission, as they produce infectious droplets ranging from 0.5 to 5 micrometers in diameter. A single sneeze can release approximately 40,000 such droplets. Historically, sneezing has been associated with divine or symbolic significance. In 410 BC, the Athenian general Xenophon interpreted a soldier's sneeze during his speech as a favorable omen from the gods, inspiring his troops to follow him. Similarly, in Homer’s Odyssey, Penelope interprets her son’s sneeze as a divine sign that Odysseus will return safely. In Japanese culture, an unexplained sneeze is often thought to mean that someone is talking about the person who sneezed. The sound of a sneeze is often represented by onomatopoeic words in different languages. In English, common representations include achoo, atisshoo, or achew. In Cypriot Greek, the sound is apshoo, which is also the name of a village. In French, the sound is atchoum, and in Japanese, it is hakushou. Cultural responses to sneezing vary widely. In English-speaking countries, it is customary to say God bless you or simply Bless you after someone sneezes. This tradition dates back to the Middle Ages, when it was believed that sneezing caused the heart to stop or the soul to leave the body, making it vulnerable to evil spirits. In other cultures, phrases related to health or well-being are used. For example, Germans say Gesundheit, meaning health, while Spanish speakers say Salud, also meaning health. In Finnish, the phrase is terveydeksi, and in Romanian, it is Sănătate or Noroc, meaning health or luck, respectively. In Hebrew, the phrase is לבריאות (labri'ut), meaning to health. In Scandinavian countries, the Latin word prosit, meaning may it benefit you, is used. In Russian, the phrase is будь здоров(а/ы) (bud zdorov), meaning be healthy. In Turkish, people say Çok yaşa, meaning live long, to which the response is Sen de gör, meaning may you see it too. In Arabic, the phrase صَحة (Sahha), meaning health, is commonly used, with responses such as شكرا (Shukran, meaning thank you) or تسلم (Taslam, meaning may you be kept safe). In French, after the first sneeze, one says à tes souhaits (to your wishes), and after a second sneeze, à tes amours (to your loves). In Islamic tradition, sneezing is accompanied by specific phrases based on Prophetic teachings. When someone sneezes, they are encouraged to say Al-hamdu-Lillaah (Praise be to Allah). In response, others say Yarhamuk Allaah (May Allah have mercy on you), to which the sneezer replies, Yahdeekum Allaah wa yuslihu baalakum (May Allah guide you and rectify your condition). Sneezing can also be caused by certain medications, such as aztreonam and oxymetazoline. Additionally, related phenomena include the photic sneeze reflex, snatiation (sneezing induced by a full stomach), and sneezing fetishism.
